You are a professional biblical lexicographer fluent in Spanish. Translate the following English lexicon entry into Spanish.

Lemma: G0142

ENGLISH GLOSSES TO TRANSLATE:
  Terse gloss: "To lift, take up, carry, or remove; spanning physical elevation, acquisition, sustained bearing, and figurative removal"
  Readable gloss: "One of the New Testament's most versatile verbs of motion, airo covers the full arc from picking something up off the ground to carrying it on one's shoulders to stripping it away entirely. Jesus commands the paralytic to 'take up' his mat (Matt 9:6), yet the same word describes God 'taking away' a fruitless branch (John 15:2). Context and voice determine whether the emphasis falls on upward movement, sustained transport, or deprivation. The nautical usage in Acts 27 and the psychological idiom in John 10:24 reveal how far a simple root of physical lifting can stretch."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "take away, remove"
    Enriched: The most frequent sense: active removal or deprivation. Spanish quitar and German aufheben confirm the 'take away' force. Covers pruning branches (John 15:2), removing privileges (Matt 21:43), and the flood 'carrying off' people (Matt 24:39). The directional focus is away-from rather than upward.
    Existing Spanish translations: Quitad, Quitaron, le-será-quitado, quita, quitad, será-quitado, te-quita
  Sense 2: "take up, pick up, gather"
    Enriched: Physical acquisition: picking up an object from where it rests. Arabic رَفَعَ and Swahili -inua both point to 'lift from the ground.' Prominent in the feeding miracles where disciples 'took up' leftover fragments (Matt 14:20, 15:37), and in Jesus' command to take up one's bed (Matt 9:6).
    Existing Spanish translations: Toma, a-tomar, a-tomarlas, habiendo-tomado, levanta, levantaron, levantasteis, recogieron, toma, tomando, tomaron
  Sense 3: "lift up, raise"
    Enriched: Upward-directed elevation: lifting eyes (John 11:41), raising the voice (Luke 17:13), or heaving stones (John 8:59). Spanish alzaron and Korean 들어올리다 capture the vertical emphasis. Distinguished from sense 2 by focus on the direction of movement rather than gaining possession.
    Existing Spanish translations: Sé-quitado, alzaron, fue-levantado, fue-recogido, levantaron, levantarán, levantó, te-levantarán, toma, tomarán, tomó
  Sense 4: "carry, bear"
    Enriched: Sustained carrying of a burden. Arabic حَمَلَ (bear a load) and Swahili beba (carry) confirm this as transport, not mere pickup. Central to the discipleship call: 'let him take up his cross' (Matt 16:24, Mark 8:34). Also describes Simon of Cyrene bearing Christ's cross (Matt 27:32).
    Existing Spanish translations: llevara, lleve, siendo-cargado, tomaran, tome, toméis
  Sense 5: "be removed (passive)"
    Enriched: Passive removal or being taken away. Covers the stone being taken from the tomb (John 20:1), Paul's appeal to put away bitterness (Eph 4:31), and the cryptic citation of Isaiah in Acts 8:33. Spanish fue-quitado and German aufgehoben reflect the passive deprivation clearly.
    Existing Spanish translations: fue-quitado, fueran-quitados, quitada, sea-quitada, sea-quitado
  Sense 6: ""
    Enriched: A crowd-cry idiom demanding someone's execution or expulsion: 'Away with him!' (Luke 23:18, Acts 21:36, 22:22). Spanish Quita/Quitalo captures the imperative urgency. Functionally a hostile demand for removal of a person, distinct from quiet physical removal.
    Existing Spanish translations: Quita, Quítalo
  Sense 7: ""
    Enriched: Nautical technical usage: weighing anchor or hoisting sails. Both occurrences appear in Acts 27 during the storm voyage. English 'having weighed anchor' and Spanish habiendo-levado-anclas confirm the specialized maritime sense of lifting the anchor from the seabed to set sail.
    Existing Spanish translations: habiendo-levado-anclas, habiendo-subido
  Sense 8: ""
    Enriched: A psychological idiom: 'to hold the soul in suspense,' meaning to keep someone in anxious uncertainty. Occurs only in John 10:24 where the crowd presses Jesus for a direct messianic claim. Spanish tienes-en-suspenso captures the figurative lifting and unsettling of the mind.
    Existing Spanish translations: tienes-en-suspenso
